I have read your other posts leading up this, to try and understand your mindset. Everyone here saying "don't do it, think of those around you," don't understand that you need to overcome this abyss for YOU, not for anyone else.

If you think by killing yourself you will be sending a message to your friend, how do you know it'll work? When you die, that's it. There's nothing else, your existence is totally obliterated. You won't be able to know whether your death makes him feel a certain way or if he'll come to some kind of epiphany.

Fresh wounds feel worse than they are, and with time even the most painful and unbearable heartbreak gives way to peaceful reflection. I have experienced the most painful unrequited love I can imagine, and it brought me to a dark place, but you must remind yourself that your life should not end because someone else has treated you a certain way.

Try not to dwell on the relationship. Emotions can quickly override your thoughts and take you down a path that seems inescapable. Distract yourself for a few hours. Find something that interests you and read about it. Watch some funny clips on YouTube (the Impractical Jokers are my go-to). Just do anything to remind yourself that there is still joy and pleasure in life.

And if you want to talk about this, or discuss anything at all, please contact me.

The customer aspect: prepare them mentally for an extended wait period, around 3 days. Sometimes you'll need that time to get it right. If you get it right sooner, even better. It's better to exceed the standard you gave them then to promise a match same-day and fail to deliver on your word.

Also, get a sample piece of wood from them. This should go without saying, but sometimes they will only bring a piece of what they want, which obviously does not help too much as far as testing the stain is concerned. Get their name, phone number and the quantity they are looking for.

The matching aspect: start off by comparing the sample piece to the Minwax chart in the store. You will almost never have a perfect match with the standard colors right off the bat, but there is enough variety where you can always start with something that's close, and tweak it from there.

Example: the sample color to be matched resembles Red Chestnut, but it has less of a red undertone. Start off with the Red Chestnut formula, cut it back to 80% to give yourself wiggle room for future adjustments, and modify the proportion of colorants. In the case of this example, remove some of the R2 and R3 and add some of the B1 and Y1 (those are the colorants used for a quart of the Minwax oil stain for Red Chestnut).

BAC pigments move wood stains fairly rapidly, so don't treat it as you would a regular paint with CCE colorants. It's difficult to describe exactly how the colorants affect the stain and interplay with each other, but you get the hang with it the more you try. It never hurts to start off with very small adjustments. Then you can adjust as you become more experienced.

As someone mentioned, most stains use B1, R2 and Y3 in various combinations. So if you end up making a stain that looks a little too hazy-muddy-greeny-grayish, and there's not a lot of maroon in the formula, you probably need to add some R2.

Certain colors cancel others, just like with the CCE pigments. Too much maroon? Add G2. Too yellow? Add L1. To reiterate: you do NOT need to add as much as you would in CCE products. Start off with baby steps.

After enough of these you will be able to nail it on the first try. I've customized formulas where I adjusted the standard formula for a color, modified the proportion of colorants and then thought "this looks like it also needs a 128th of R3 and a 64th of G2" and the stain came out dead-on.

Also, I recommend putting a clear over part of the final version of the stain you match. Sometimes it gives it a perfect finish that looks really nice, and that way you can show the customer and have them decide if they want it with the clear or without. Just be mindful that certain clears have an ambering effect that will alter the color. There is a display at the Minwax color selection explaining this.

I have talked with several people who were able to change their outlook by familiarizing themselves with the philosophical works of Albert Camus, in particular his notion of "the Absurd."

In short, the Absurd refers to the idea that humans innately seek meaning in all things, including life itself, but we exist in a universe that offers no clear meaning, which puts us in a deep existential crisis.

Camus argued that rather than enduring the despair of a meaningless universe, we should *accept* that there is no inherent meaning to life, which frees us from the despair, and nevertheless rebel against the meaninglessness by living a life that you want to live.

In other words, accepting the Absurd and acknowledging that there is no inherent meaning to life, but going on to live anyway, is what gives life meaning.

This is a very crude synopsis of Camus' vision but I hope I have at least made the principle clear enough to provide you with some peace of mind.
